3  Shortcut Solvability


A benchmark score is evidence of capability only if every policy that reaches a comparable score
has the capability. We call a policy that reaches the score while lacking the capability a shortcut,
and a benchmark shortcut-solvable when one exists.

LIBERO [2] is a language-conditioned manipulation benchmark that tests lifelong learning across
language-specified tasks. Scoring well is meant to require understanding the instruction, yet a high
score is read as evidence of much more. Because the top of its leaderboard is held by foundation
VLAs, a high score is taken to show that the policy generalizes broadly, and that reaching it requires
large-scale robotics pretraining and a large, expressive model.

We test whether a high score can be reached without those properties. Our probe is a deliberately
small model with approximately 90M parameters (a shared DINOv2 encoder [34] and a small MLP
head), with no language encoder, no large-scale robotics pretraining, and no expressive action head
(i.e., no diffusion head or action tokenizer). Because each benchmark draws its instructions from a
fixed public set, the probe replaces the instruction with a learned per-task embedding that it looks up
by index instead of reading as text. On LIBERO each instruction maps to its own embedding, and
on CALVIN several phrasings of a subtask map to the same embedding. The probe uses only what
each benchmark’s evaluation protocol lets any policy use, so reaching its score this way reveals a
weakness in the protocol, not a trick of ours.

Table 1 shows that LIBERO is shortcut-solvable since the probe performs within one percentage
point of the best published result on three of four splits.1 On CALVIN, the shortcut is real but
smaller, since the probe matches the performance of widely-used policies but not the current best.
On RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa, and SimplerEnv, the probe scores well below the best, indicating the
lack of a shortcut.

We claim only that a high score on LIBERO is not, on its own, evidence of general manipulation
capability—our probe achieves a high score yet lacks such a capability. We do not claim that a
high-scoring policy lacks that capability, since a capable policy reaches a high score too. 2

4   Statistical Significance


When a new policy is published, it will often report a higher aggregate benchmark score than the
previous best from the literature, and that gap is taken as progress. In this section, we consider the
question of determining how statistically significant such performance gaps may be.

Most papers report only an aggregate score, most commonly an average success rate. However,
the aggregate score alone is often not enough to determine the statistical significance of a reported
performance gap, a gap we then call inconclusive.  It arises because the variance of the empiri-
cally observed performance gap is a function of task-level and sample-level information that is not
retained by the average performance statistic (Appendix C).

The paired Wald statistic cannot be computed from top-line metrics alone. Lacking access to the full
paired outcome data, we derive two cutoffs on the reported empirical gap. The rejection-feasibility
threshold δ∃(bµA; T, S, R, α) is chosen so that if b∆< δ∃(bµA; T, S, R, α), then no paired outcome
table compatible with the reported top-line metrics can reject the null hypothesis. The rejection-
guarantee threshold δ∀(bµA; T, S, R, α) is chosen such that b∆≥δ∀(bµA; T, S, R, α), implies that
every paired outcome table compatible with the reported top-line metrics rejects the null hypothesis.
The derivation is given in Appendix C.

For paired evaluations, these top-line bounds are sharp. Below the feasibility threshold, rejection is
impossible from the reported aggregate scores. Above the guarantee threshold, rejection is forced
by the reported aggregate scores. Between the corresponding pointwise feasibility and guarantee
conditions, the aggregate scores alone do not determine significance: the same reported counts are
compatible with paired outcome tables that reject and with paired outcome tables that do not reject.

Some audited papers do not evaluate both policies on the same benchmark instances, choosing
instead to evaluate on iid samples drawn from the benchmark distribution. For these comparisons,
the natural reference procedure is a stratified two-sample Wald test rather than the paired Wald
test above. We still use the paired envelopes as conservative top-line cutoffs, but in such cases the
thresholds will no longer be sharp.

5  Creeping Overfitting

A benchmark has a fixed and usually narrow test distribution (for example, over object types, object
poses, backgrounds, and camera poses).  Its official test set is a set of finite samples drawn from
that distribution. Over time, models can become too tuned to the benchmark rather than acquiring
broader manipulation skill, which prior work calls creeping overfitting [11]. Fitting to the narrow
test distribution is distribution overfitting, and fitting to the fixed samples is sample overfitting.

Distribution overfitting. CALVIN’s most commonly used protocol, ABC→D, trains on three table
scenes (A, B, C) and tests on a fourth held-out scene D, where each evaluation episode is a chain of
five language-conditioned tasks scored as the average number completed (ATC). During training the
table blocks can start at any pose in a range, but the released scene-D evaluation fixes them at the
same poses. We resampled the block poses from that same training range and held everything else
fixed. ATC fell by 1.03 for X-VLA [35], 0.75 for GR-1 [36], and 0.50 for RoboFlamingo [37] with

## 1. cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 10-11 (Context ID: pqac-00000046)

er different conditions in terms of spatial ar-
rangement (LIBERO-SPATIAL), object considerd (LIBERO-OBJECT), and overall task variations
(LIBERO-GOAL). LIBERO does also provide a benchmark for continuing, short (LIBERO-90)
and long-horizon (LIBERO-LONG) tasks requiring the transfer of entangled knowledge between
the aforementioned sources of variation. Typical LIBERO evaluation protocols report the success
rate over a number of test episodes, and lerobot natively integrates LIBERO.


Meta-World  Similarly to LIBERO, Meta-World was first developed as a benchmark for assess-
ing the performance of generic autonomous systems, with a particular focus on fast adaptation to
novel scenarios via meta-learning. Adapting quickly to novel scenarios is a particularly promis-
ing area of research in the field of robotics, as it holds the premise of enabling the development of
systems that can effectively generalize to unseen tasks leveraging previously acquired information.
The Meta-World benchmark consists of 50 distinct robotic manipulation tasks that can be combined
into different benchmark suites. The benchmark is structured to quantify performance under dif-
ferent learning regimes: multi-task learning (MT10, MT50) where the agent learns multiple tasks
simultaneously with access to a task identifier, and meta-learning (ML1, ML10, ML45) which as-
sesses the agent’s ability to adapt to new tasks using minimal data. All 50 different tasks require
the same robotic arm in the same setup to interact with multiple objects with different shapes and
diverse uses. Critically, all the high-level tasks presented in Meta-World require the robot to execute
a combination of fixed, more fundamental skills such as reaching for an object or manipulating it.
Such a common task conceptual structure proves instrumental in providing a shared interface for
autonomous agents to use and learn how to transfer knowledge across different tasks: a key property
of the adaptability that is required of modern robot policies (Black et al., 2024; Shukor et al., 2025).


5  CONCLUSIONS

In this work we introduced lerobot, a unified, open-source stack for end-to-end robot learning that
bridges low-level control, large-scale data tooling, and scalable learning algorithms. We showed how
accessible teleoperation of multiple real-world robot through a shared middleware can be used to
collect real-world data across a variety of robot platforms. Further, we illustrated how standardized
datasets can be exploited to collect and reuse data at scale, powering advancements in robot learning
thanks to the thousands of datasets collected, resulting in hundreds of thousands of episodic data,
and hundreds of models openly contributed by the robot learning community.


Limitations  We identify several limitations remaining in our contribution. First, robots coverage
is currently far from exhaustive, as we support a practical but incomplete set of arms, grippers, sen-
sors, and controllers. Over the course of 2025, lerobot went from supporting 3 manipulation
setups (Koch-v1.1, SO-100, ALOHA) to the 8 regular, humanoid and mobile manipulators cur-
rently supported, and we highlight that keeping a similar rate of progress is paramount to properly
serve the robot learning community. Second, the coverage in terms of robot learning algorithms is
also non-exhaustive. We provide strong, reproducible implementations across key paradigms, while
extending the library with additional algorithms remains future work. Third, achieving strong prac-
tical inference performance still requires low-level optimization (quantization, graph compilation,
etc) that are currently disregarded by the library. We view these limitations as concrete, tractable
avenues for community contributions and future development, and in the very spirit of open-source,
invite the broader robot learning community to address them. However, despite these limitations,
our work takes a significant step toward an end-to-end stack for robot learning, providing a useful
tool for researchers and practioners in the field.

27       1  Introduction

           Real-world evaluation increasingly gates progress in generalist robot manipulation. Assessing com-
           petence requires physical hardware, varied trials, and an operator to arrange, reset, and score each
             rollout. The resulting cost limits many studies to a few dozen trials on one robot in one lab, making
          improvements hard to distinguish from noise and results hard to compare. Unreported choices such[cs.RO]
            as camera placement, lighting, object initialisation, checkpoint selection, and task-speciﬁc tuning
          can further inﬂate headline success rates and hinder independent reproduction (Atreya et al., 2025).
              Simulation makes evaluation cheap and reproducible but inherits a sim-to-real gap. Physical
          benchmarks avoid that gap, but often trade cost for fewer tasks or trials, a single embodiment, or
            coarse binary scoring. ArmnetBench instead reduces the per-trial cost with parallel low-cost cells.
          Each adds three cameras, a Raspberry Pi, and a networked power plug to the largely 3D-printable
          SO-101 (Cadène et al., 2024).  The farm runs policy rollouts in isolated containers under one
            protocol. This supports broad coverage across tasks, policies as well as single-arm and bimanual
           conﬁgurations, with every scored rollout released as data.
               v0.1 validates this evaluation substrate and establishes a baseline for iteration. Its leaderboard
          compares policies trained or ﬁne-tuned on the same 50 demonstrations per task; it does not estimate

2  Related Work

Simulation and task-suite benchmarks. Simulated suites make manipulation evaluation cheap
and parallel. Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020) covers multi-task and meta-RL manipulation, LIBERO (Liu
et al., 2023) targets lifelong-learning transfer, and SIMPLER (Li et al., 2024) seeks rankings that
align with real robots. Contact, deformables, and visual realism still transfer imperfectly, motivat-
ing evaluation on physical robots.
   Reproducible real-world benchmarks. Physical benchmarks standardise hardware or scenes.
REPLAB (Yang et al., 2019) provides a reproducible low-cost cell, SceneReplica (Khargonkar et al.,
2024) replicable scenes, FurnitureBench (Heo et al., 2025) long-horizon assembly, FMB (Luo et al.,
2025) functional manipulation, and VLA-REPLICA (Huang et al., 2026) a replicable SO-101 cell
for cross-lab VLA evaluation. These are primarily blueprints for independently rebuilt setups.
   Auto-evaluation and distributed evaluation. AutoEval (Zhou et al., 2025) automates reset
and success detection on one robot. RoboArena (Atreya et al., 2025) pools heterogeneous labs and
uses preference scoring because absolute rates do not compare across sites. RoboDojo (Chen et al.,
2026) combines simulation with a standardised remote service on bimanual platforms.
   Low-cost arms and datasets. ALOHA (Zhao et al., 2023) showed that low-cost hardware
can support ﬁne-grained bimanual manipulation.  Large-scale datasets such as DROID (Khaz-
atsky et al., 2024) collect diverse real-world interactions, while Open X-Embodiment (Open X-
Embodiment Collaboration, 2024) aggregates data across robot embodiments. LeRobot (Cadène
et al., 2024) provides open hardware, software, and dataset tooling around low-cost arms including
the SO-100/SO-101.
   Together, these lines of work address simulation, reproducible hardware, automated or dis-
tributed evaluation, and scalable data collection. ArmnetBench combines a managed low-cost ﬂeet
with same-cell policy comparison and a released, graded evaluation corpus (Table 1). Whether

3  The Armnet Arm Farm

We collect ArmnetBench v0.1 on the Armnet arm farm: a managed ﬂeet of low-cost single-arm
and bimanual SO-101 cells. In v0.1, one co-located workstation builds and runs policy containers,
performs inference and real-time control, and drives the arms over the local network. A cloud
backend schedules jobs and streams logs and video for operator monitoring.

## pqac-00000058

From text 'selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9'.

Praveen Selvaraj, Lorenzo Uttini, and Ville Kuosmanen. Armnetbench v0.1: parallel real-world evaluation of manipulation policies on a low-cost arm farm. ArXiv, Jul 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481. This article has 4 citations.

The excerpt describes ArmnetBench v0.1 as a real-world evaluation on low-cost parallel SO-101 arm cells, conducted under light on-site supervision. It evaluates 12 manipulation tasks: eight single-arm tasks and four bimanual tasks. The protocol uses a common 50-demonstration training budget for every policy, followed by scored rollouts for each task–policy pairing. Per-task results generally aggregate 30 rollouts; two pairings have 29 after data cleaning because of excluded episodes caused by incorrect scene resets. The primary metric is strict success rate: only rollouts judged successful are counted. A secondary “success+suboptimal” metric additionally credits poor-quality but completed executions. The compared policies are ACT, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, MolmoAct 2, GR00T N1.7, and Diffusion Policy. The excerpt gives task-level success percentages and an overall pooled leaderboard, while noting that results are embodiment-dependent and should not be extrapolated between single-arm and bimanual settings. It also identifies evaluation caveats, including operator-dependent stopping, unmeasured initial-state variation, object wear, and some camera issues across physical cells.


---

## pqac-00000059

From text 'selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7'.

Praveen Selvaraj, Lorenzo Uttini, and Ville Kuosmanen. Armnetbench v0.1: parallel real-world evaluation of manipulation policies on a low-cost arm farm. ArXiv, Jul 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481. This article has 4 citations.

ArmnetBench v0.1 evaluates manipulation policies on SO-101 follower-arm cells, using two single-arm cells and one bimanual cell in the reported deployment. The benchmark contains 12 tabletop tasks—8 single-arm and 4 bimanual—covering stacking, insertion, deformable objects, pick-and-place, and articulated-object manipulation. Each task-policy combination is evaluated for 30 rollouts, with two episodes removed because of incorrect manual resets, leaving those particular pairs with 29. Before every rollout, an operator resets the scene and randomizes object placement within a task-specific range; initial states are sampled independently rather than matched across policies. Each policy is trained or fine-tuned for the task using the same 50 human-teleoperated demonstrations. Rollouts use three synchronized camera views at 20 fps, and the operator assigns one of three labels: successful when the task goal is achieved cleanly, suboptimal when achieved with a poor-quality finish, or failure when the goal is not achieved. Seven policies are compared: ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, and MolmoAct 2.


---

## pqac-00000060

From text 'selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3'.

Praveen Selvaraj, Lorenzo Uttini, and Ville Kuosmanen. Armnetbench v0.1: parallel real-world evaluation of manipulation policies on a low-cost arm farm. ArXiv, Jul 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481. This article has 4 citations.

ArmnetBench v0.1 evaluates manipulation policies on a managed fleet of low-cost SO-101 cells, supporting both single-arm and bimanual configurations. Each cell has one or two 5-DoF follower arms, three cameras, a Raspberry Pi 5 edge device, and a fixed workspace; object positions are randomized between rollouts. Policies run in isolated containers under a shared protocol, with one workstation handling inference and real-time control and a cloud backend scheduling jobs and streaming logs and video for monitoring. The benchmark covers 12 tasks and compares 7 policies. Every policy is trained or fine-tuned using 50 demonstrations per task. It contains 2,518 policy rollouts plus 600 reference demonstrations, for 3,118 total core episodes. Since 2,518 divided across 12 tasks and 7 policy-task combinations is approximately 30, the excerpt suggests about 30 evaluation rollouts per task per policy, although it does not explicitly state this allocation. Rollouts are scored by operators using three labels: successful, suboptimal, or failure; demonstrations are successful by construction. The excerpt does not identify the seven policies by name or provide the detailed task-specific success criteria.

FurnitureBench reports success rates as percentages, with the single-skill benchmark averaging results over 10 trials. For each trial, the robot arm first moves to its initial pose. The furniture parts are then rearranged with the provided tool according to the selected initialization level. A policy controls the robot until the task is completed or an evaluation termination condition occurs: the robot stops moving for 5 seconds, exhibits unsafe movements, exceeds 350 steps for an individual skill, or exceeds 3000 total steps. Afterward, both the success rate and phase-completion score are recorded. For the simulation benchmark, FurnitureSim evaluates policies on the one_leg assembly task and measures both success rates and average completed phases, comparing behavioral cloning and offline reinforcement learning methods with visual encoders. {"answer": "# Reliability Statistics for Robot Manipulation: Reporting Success Rates, Confidence Intervals, and Mean Cycles Between Interventions

## 1. The Problem: How the Field Currently Reports Success

The dominant metric in physical robot-manipulation evaluation is "success rate"—the percentage of autonomous runs that succeed. Kress-Gazit et al. (2024, preprint) argue that this practice is insufficient: "it is common for papers to report this number with little to no information regarding the number of runs, the initial conditions, and the success criteria, little to no narrative description of the behaviors and failures observed, and little to no statistical analysis of the findings" (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012). A recent audit of the five most-cited manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0) found that the majority of reported performance gaps between policies are statistically inconclusive when examined with paired Wald tests: across LIBERO, only 20.8% of 789 comparisons were provably significant at the 5% level (pqac-00000042).

The following table summarizes how major benchmarks actually report results, their trial counts, and whether they include any form of uncertainty estimate.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 2. Binomial Confidence Intervals for Binary Task Success

### 2.1 Framing the Problem

Each manipulation trial is naturally modeled as a Bernoulli random variable X ∈ {0,1} with unknown success probability p (pqac-00000007). The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol defines reliability as "the probability of successfully completing a task or sub-task," computed from "a confidence level (CL), the number of successes (m), and the number of independent trials (n)" using the binomial cumulative distribution function (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000037). This requires independent, identically distributed trials—a condition that Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L) emphasize must be ensured by a pre-specified testing plan, warning that practices such as "running policy rollouts until enough favorable outcomes are observed" violate the i.i.d. assumption (pqac-00000040).

### 2.2 Clopper–Pearson (Exact) Intervals

The Clopper–Pearson method inverts exact binomial tail probabilities to produce a confidence interval whose coverage is guaranteed to be at least 1−α for all values of p (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055). The two-sided 100(1−α)% interval allocates α/2 to each tail. Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics) characterizes Clopper–Pearson as "very conservative" because its actual coverage typically exceeds the nominal level, especially at small sample sizes; mean coverage at n=15 with nominal 95% was measured at 0.974 (pqac-00000056). Vincent et al. (2024) note that the Clopper–Pearson lower bound is obtained from their uniformly most accurate (UMA) framework by "setting U = 0 in the test statistic," confirming it as a special case of the optimal bound and showing that their randomized UMA bound is always tighter (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000051).

### 2.3 Wilson Score Intervals

Wilson score intervals provide better-behaved coverage than the normal-approximation (Wald) interval, particularly when p is near 0 or 1 or when sample sizes are small (pqac-00000016). The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark (Vagas et al. 2026, IEEE RA-L) explicitly states that "we report Wilson score confidence intervals, which offer [well-behaved coverage] when sample sizes are small or observed proportions are close to 0 or 1" (pqac-00000016). Wilson intervals are increasingly adopted in 2025–2026 manipulation papers: Zhang et al. (2025, preprint) report "Wilson-score 95% confidence intervals for SR [success rate]" on their Mobile ALOHA VLA benchmarking (pqac-00000023); SafeVLA-Bench uses "Wilson score 95% intervals for binomial proportions"; and LADDER reports "95% Wilson confidence intervals over episodes."

Orawo (2021) recommends Wilson and likelihood intervals over both Wald and Clopper–Pearson for practical use, because they achieve near-nominal coverage without the excessive conservatism of the exact method (pqac-00000056).

### 2.4 Bayesian Approach

Kress-Gazit et al. (2024) illustrate a Bayesian alternative: model success as a Bernoulli distribution with unknown probability, place a uniform prior, and inspect the posterior distribution. They demonstrate that two policies achieving 13/20 (65%) and 14/20 (70%) have substantially overlapping posteriors, yielding only a 0.11 probability that the inferior policy is truly better—emphasizing that identical percentages from small samples cannot support superiority claims (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010).

## 3. Minimum Number of Trials for Reliability Claims

The central sample-size question for robot reliability is: if all n trials succeed, how large must n be to claim that p ≥ p₀ with confidence 1−α? The exact one-sided binomial answer is n ≥ ⌈ln(α)/ln(p₀)⌉ (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053). For the canonical claim of "at least 95% success with 95% confidence," this yields n = ⌈ln(0.05)/ln(0.95)⌉ = ⌈58.40⌉ = 59 trials with zero failures. The well-known "rule of three" approximates this as 3/(1−p₀) = 60 (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). If a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval is required instead, the lower tail uses α/2 = 0.025, yielding n = ⌈ln(0.025)/ln(0.95)⌉ = 72 (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000053).

The following table provides the exact trial counts for several practically relevant reliability targets.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Critical implication for low-cost arms:** Most published manipulation papers use far fewer trials than the 59 required for a one-sided 95%/95% claim. ALOHA uses 25 real-robot trials per task (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028); Mobile ALOHA uses 20 (pqac-00000024); FurnitureBench uses 10 (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062); YCB protocols use 10 (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015); and ArmnetBench uses 30 (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059). With 25 all-success trials, the one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson lower bound on p is only 0.05^(1/25) ≈ 0.887, not 0.95. To genuinely certify 95% success at 95% confidence, 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are necessary.

## 4. Mean Cycles Between Interventions and MTBF

### 4.1 In Lab Automation

Laboratory automation systems report reliability using mean time between failures (MTBF) measured in calendar days or operating hours. Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection, peer-reviewed) report that BD Kiestra TLA and WCA automated bacteriology systems achieve approximately 100 days MTBF, while the Copan WASPLab achieves approximately 95 days, with the caveat that "MTBF is difficult to specify because it depends substantially on system configuration, overall system complexity, the number and variety of samples processed each day, and user-induced factors" (pqac-00000030). In industrial manufacturing with Digital Twin/IIoT-enabled predictive maintenance, Mostofa (2024) reports baseline MTBF of 1,486.3 hours (SD 412.7; 95% CI [1,431.5, 1,541.1]) across 220 assets including robotic systems, improving to 2,176.8 hours post-intervention (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033).

### 4.2 In Field Robotics

Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology, peer-reviewed) note that "the Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) for robots in field environments is often within a few hours" (pqac-00000049), highlighting the substantial gap between industrial automation and research robot reliability.

### 4.3 Explicit Gap: No Standard for Mean Cycles Between Interventions in Manipulation

**No published standard exists for reporting "mean cycles between interventions" (MCBI) as a reliability metric for robot manipulation tasks.** The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol uses binomial success probability and completion time (mean, SD, and 95% CI), but does not define a cycles-between-interventions metric (pqac-00000037). Lab automation papers report MTBF in time units rather than task cycles (pqac-00000030). For teams running repeated pick-and-place or assembly cycles on low-cost arms, defining and reporting MCBI—the mean number of autonomous task cycles completed before a human must intervene to reset, fix a jam, or correct an error—would fill a genuine gap in the literature. This metric can be modeled as a geometric or negative-binomial random variable and reported with appropriate confidence intervals.

## 5. Best Practices for Reporting: A Synthesis

Based on the surveyed literature, the following reporting practices are recommended for teams benchmarking low-cost arms:

**What to report for each task:**
1. **Raw counts:** Report k successes out of n trials, not just percentages (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012).
2. **Confidence interval:** Report a Wilson score 95% CI for each success proportion (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023), or a Clopper–Pearson interval if conservative coverage is preferred (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). If using Bayesian methods, show posterior distributions (pqac-00000003).
3. **Success criterion:** Define success semantically and unambiguously. The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark defines success as "lifting the object at least 5 cm within 3 seconds and holding it for 3 seconds without slipping, with a 10-second timeout" (pqac-00000016). FurnitureBench uses phase-completion scores alongside binary success (pqac-00000062). ArmnetBench uses three-way grading: successful, suboptimal, or failure (pqac-00000058).
4. **Initial conditions:** Specify the randomization range, whether initial conditions are matched across policies, and whether evaluations are interleaved (pqac-00000013).
5. **Failure modes:** Describe observed failure modes qualitatively (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012).
6. **Completion time:** Report mean, standard deviation, and 95% CI for task-completion time (pqac-00000037).
7. **Trial independence:** Verify and state that trials are independent—no cherry-picking, no stopping-when-good, no environmental drift (pqac-00000040).

**How many trials to run:**
- For a **screening evaluation** during development: 20–30 trials per task are standard practice (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000058) and will give Wilson 95% CI half-widths of roughly ±15–20 percentage points at 80% success.
- For a **formal reliability claim** of p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence: 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are required (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052).
- For **comparing two policies:** Use at least 20 trials per policy under matched initial conditions and apply a paired test or Bayesian comparison (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000010). Jiang et al. (2026, preprint) show that even with hundreds of comparisons, reported performance gaps are often statistically inconclusive (pqac-00000042).

## 6. Placing Low-Cost Arms in the Published Literature

### 6.1 Available Benchmarks for SO-101 and ALOHA-Class Arms

**ArmnetBench v0.1** (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint) is the most directly relevant benchmark for SO-101 arms. It evaluates 7 policies (ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct 2) across 12 tasks on a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, using 30 rollouts per task-policy pair with 50 demonstrations and three-way operator scoring (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060).

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al. 2026, ICLR, peer-reviewed) provides the open-source software stack supporting SO-100, SO-101, Koch-v1.1, and ALOHA hardware. It integrates LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks and standardized dataset formats, but the paper itself does not report real-world success-rate benchmarks with confidence intervals for specific arms (pqac-00000046).

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) provides a multi-embodiment dataset spanning Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, AgileX dual-arm robot, and a humanoid, with 107k demonstrations across 479 tasks, enabling cross-embodiment comparison.

### 6.2 Explicit Gaps

- **No published peer-reviewed paper benchmarks the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm** on any standard manipulation protocol with reported confidence intervals. Any reliability claim for PiPER would need to be generated de novo.
- **No published paper provides a head-to-head reliability comparison** (with binomial confidence intervals or MTBF) between low-cost arms (SO-101, PiPER, ALOHA) and industrial arms (UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) on matched tasks. RoboMIND includes multiple embodiments but reports imitation-learning success rates rather than hardware-reliability metrics.
- **ABB YuMi** and **Kinova** arms appear in the manipulation literature but not in published benchmarks with the statistical rigor described here.

### 6.3 Repeatable Protocol Recommendation

For teams with PiPER and SO-101 arms seeking to generate publishable, comparable data:

1. **Select a standard object set** (YCB objects are freely available with 3D models) (pqac-00000015).
2. **Use the NIST Assembly Task Board protocol** for assembly tasks: record start/finish times, autonomous operation only (no manual intervention permitted), and report binomial reliability bounds (pqac-00000037).
3. **For imitation-learning policies**, follow the ArmnetBench protocol: 50 demonstrations, 30+ rollouts per task-policy pair, three-way scoring, randomized initial placement (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059).
4. **Report Wilson score 95% CIs** for all success proportions, state the one-sided or two-sided convention, and report raw k/n alongside percentages.
5. **For reliability certification**, run at least 59 consecutive successful trials per task to claim p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052).
6. **For comparing with Franka or UR5e results**, use matched tasks from FMB (25 trials, Franka), FurnitureBench (10 trials, Franka Panda), or RoboMIND protocols and recompute confidence intervals on the published raw counts.

## 7. Publication Status of Cited Sources

The following papers cited in this review are **preprints** (not yet peer-reviewed in a journal or major conference proceedings): Kress-Gazit et al. (2024), Jiang et al. (2026), Selvaraj et al. (2026, ArmnetBench), Wu et al. (2024, RoboMIND), Zhao et al. (2023, ALOHA), Fu et al. (2024, Mobile ALOHA), Zhang et al. (2025, Experiences Benchmarking VLA), Fan et al. (2026, SafeVLA-Bench), Zha et al. (2026, LAP), Petkov et al. (2026, LADDER), and Chen et al. (2026, RoboDojo). The following are **peer-reviewed**: Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L), Kimble et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L), Calli et al. (2015, IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine), Vagas et al. (2026, IEEE RA-L), Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics), Heo et al. (2025, IJRR), Luo et al. (2024, IJRR), Denoun et al. (2023, IEEE Transactions on Robotics), Morgan et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L), Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection), Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology), Cadène et al. (2026, ICLR), and Budde et al. (2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science)."}

The Clopper–Pearson method inverts exact binomial tail probabilities to produce a confidence interval whose coverage is guaranteed to be at least 1−α for all values of p (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055). The two-sided 100(1−α)% interval allocates α/2 to each tail. Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics) characterizes Clopper–Pearson as "very conservative" because its actual coverage typically exceeds the nominal level, especially at small sample sizes; mean coverage at n=15 with nominal 95% was measured at 0.974 (pqac-00000056). Vincent et al. (2024) note that the Clopper–Pearson lower bound is obtained from their uniformly most accurate (UMA) framework by "setting U = 0 in the test statistic," confirming it as a special case of the optimal bound and showing that their randomized UMA bound is always tighter (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000051).

### 2.3 Wilson Score Intervals

Wilson score intervals provide better-behaved coverage than the normal-approximation (Wald) interval, particularly when p is near 0 or 1 or when sample sizes are small (pqac-00000016). The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark (Vagas et al. 2026, IEEE RA-L) explicitly states that "we report Wilson score confidence intervals, which offer [well-behaved coverage] when sample sizes are small or observed proportions are close to 0 or 1" (pqac-00000016). Wilson intervals are increasingly adopted in 2025–2026 manipulation papers: Zhang et al. (2025, preprint) report "Wilson-score 95% confidence intervals for SR [success rate]" on their Mobile ALOHA VLA benchmarking (pqac-00000023); SafeVLA-Bench uses "Wilson score 95% intervals for binomial proportions"; and LADDER reports "95% Wilson confidence intervals over episodes."

Orawo (2021) recommends Wilson and likelihood intervals over both Wald and Clopper–Pearson for practical use, because they achieve near-nominal coverage without the excessive conservatism of the exact method (pqac-00000056).

### 2.4 Bayesian Approach

Kress-Gazit et al. (2024) illustrate a Bayesian alternative: model success as a Bernoulli distribution with unknown probability, place a uniform prior, and inspect the posterior distribution. They demonstrate that two policies achieving 13/20 (65%) and 14/20 (70%) have substantially overlapping posteriors, yielding only a 0.11 probability that the inferior policy is truly better—emphasizing that identical percentages from small samples cannot support superiority claims (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010).

## 3. Minimum Number of Trials for Reliability Claims

The central sample-size question for robot reliability is: if all n trials succeed, how large must n be to claim that p ≥ p₀ with confidence 1−α? The exact one-sided binomial answer is n ≥ ⌈ln(α)/ln(p₀)⌉ (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053). For the canonical claim of "at least 95% success with 95% confidence," this yields n = ⌈ln(0.05)/ln(0.95)⌉ = ⌈58.40⌉ = 59 trials with zero failures. The well-known "rule of three" approximates this as 3/(1−p₀) = 60 (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). If a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval is required instead, the lower tail uses α/2 = 0.025, yielding n = ⌈ln(0.025)/ln(0.95)⌉ = 72 (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000053).

The following table provides the exact trial counts for several practically relevant reliability targets.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Critical implication for low-cost arms:** Most published manipulation papers use far fewer trials than the 59 required for a one-sided 95%/95% claim. ALOHA uses 25 real-robot trials per task (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028); Mobile ALOHA uses 20 (pqac-00000024); FurnitureBench uses 10 (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062); YCB protocols use 10 (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015); and ArmnetBench uses 30 (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059). With 25 all-success trials, the one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson lower bound on p is only 0.05^(1/25) ≈ 0.887, not 0.95. To genuinely certify 95% success at 95% confidence, 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are necessary.

## 4. Mean Cycles Between Interventions and MTBF

### 4.1 In Lab Automation

Laboratory automation systems report reliability using mean time between failures (MTBF) measured in calendar days or operating hours. Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection, peer-reviewed) report that BD Kiestra TLA and WCA automated bacteriology systems achieve approximately 100 days MTBF, while the Copan WASPLab achieves approximately 95 days, with the caveat that "MTBF is difficult to specify because it depends substantially on system configuration, overall system complexity, the number and variety of samples processed each day, and user-induced factors" (pqac-00000030). In industrial manufacturing with Digital Twin/IIoT-enabled predictive maintenance, Mostofa (2024) reports baseline MTBF of 1,486.3 hours (SD 412.7; 95% CI [1,431.5, 1,541.1]) across 220 assets including robotic systems, improving to 2,176.8 hours post-intervention (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033).

### 4.2 In Field Robotics

Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology, peer-reviewed) note that "the Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) for robots in field environments is often within a few hours" (pqac-00000049), highlighting the substantial gap between industrial automation and research robot reliability.

### 4.3 Explicit Gap: No Standard for Mean Cycles Between Interventions in Manipulation

**No published standard exists for reporting "mean cycles between interventions" (MCBI) as a reliability metric for robot manipulation tasks.** The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol uses binomial success probability and completion time (mean, SD, and 95% CI), but does not define a cycles-between-interventions metric (pqac-00000037). Lab automation papers report MTBF in time units rather than task cycles (pqac-00000030). For teams running repeated pick-and-place or assembly cycles on low-cost arms, defining and reporting MCBI—the mean number of autonomous task cycles completed before a human must intervene to reset, fix a jam, or correct an error—would fill a genuine gap in the literature. This metric can be modeled as a geometric or negative-binomial random variable and reported with appropriate confidence intervals.

## 5. Best Practices for Reporting: A Synthesis

Based on the surveyed literature, the following reporting practices are recommended for teams benchmarking low-cost arms:

**What to report for each task:**
1. **Raw counts:** Report k successes out of n trials, not just percentages (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012).
2. **Confidence interval:** Report a Wilson score 95% CI for each success proportion (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023), or a Clopper–Pearson interval if conservative coverage is preferred (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). If using Bayesian methods, show posterior distributions (pqac-00000003).
3. **Success criterion:** Define success semantically and unambiguously. The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark defines success as "lifting the object at least 5 cm within 3 seconds and holding it for 3 seconds without slipping, with a 10-second timeout" (pqac-00000016). FurnitureBench uses phase-completion scores alongside binary success (pqac-00000062). ArmnetBench uses three-way grading: successful, suboptimal, or failure (pqac-00000058).
4. **Initial conditions:** Specify the randomization range, whether initial conditions are matched across policies, and whether evaluations are interleaved (pqac-00000013).
5. **Failure modes:** Describe observed failure modes qualitatively (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012).
6. **Completion time:** Report mean, standard deviation, and 95% CI for task-completion time (pqac-00000037).
7. **Trial independence:** Verify and state that trials are independent—no cherry-picking, no stopping-when-good, no environmental drift (pqac-00000040).

**How many trials to run:**
- For a **screening evaluation** during development: 20–30 trials per task are standard practice (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000058) and will give Wilson 95% CI half-widths of roughly ±15–20 percentage points at 80% success.
- For a **formal reliability claim** of p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence: 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are required (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052).
- For **comparing two policies:** Use at least 20 trials per policy under matched initial conditions and apply a paired test or Bayesian comparison (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000010). Jiang et al. (2026, preprint) show that even with hundreds of comparisons, reported performance gaps are often statistically inconclusive (pqac-00000042).

## 6. Placing Low-Cost Arms in the Published Literature

### 6.1 Available Benchmarks for SO-101 and ALOHA-Class Arms

**ArmnetBench v0.1** (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint) is the most directly relevant benchmark for SO-101 arms. It evaluates 7 policies (ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct 2) across 12 tasks on a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, using 30 rollouts per task-policy pair with 50 demonstrations and three-way operator scoring (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060).

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al. 2026, ICLR, peer-reviewed) provides the open-source software stack supporting SO-100, SO-101, Koch-v1.1, and ALOHA hardware. It integrates LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks and standardized dataset formats, but the paper itself does not report real-world success-rate benchmarks with confidence intervals for specific arms (pqac-00000046).

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) provides a multi-embodiment dataset spanning Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, AgileX dual-arm robot, and a humanoid, with 107k demonstrations across 479 tasks, enabling cross-embodiment comparison.

### 6.2 Explicit Gaps

- **No published peer-reviewed paper benchmarks the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm** on any standard manipulation protocol with reported confidence intervals. Any reliability claim for PiPER would need to be generated de novo.
- **No published paper provides a head-to-head reliability comparison** (with binomial confidence intervals or MTBF) between low-cost arms (SO-101, PiPER, ALOHA) and industrial arms (UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) on matched tasks. RoboMIND includes multiple embodiments but reports imitation-learning success rates rather than hardware-reliability metrics.
- **ABB YuMi** and **Kinova** arms appear in the manipulation literature but not in published benchmarks with the statistical rigor described here.

### 6.3 Repeatable Protocol Recommendation

For teams with PiPER and SO-101 arms seeking to generate publishable, comparable data:

1. **Select a standard object set** (YCB objects are freely available with 3D models) (pqac-00000015).
2. **Use the NIST Assembly Task Board protocol** for assembly tasks: record start/finish times, autonomous operation only (no manual intervention permitted), and report binomial reliability bounds (pqac-00000037).
3. **For imitation-learning policies**, follow the ArmnetBench protocol: 50 demonstrations, 30+ rollouts per task-policy pair, three-way scoring, randomized initial placement (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059).
4. **Report Wilson score 95% CIs** for all success proportions, state the one-sided or two-sided convention, and report raw k/n alongside percentages.
5. **For reliability certification**, run at least 59 consecutive successful trials per task to claim p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052).
6. **For comparing with Franka or UR5e results**, use matched tasks from FMB (25 trials, Franka), FurnitureBench (10 trials, Franka Panda), or RoboMIND protocols and recompute confidence intervals on the published raw counts.

## 7. Publication Status of Cited Sources

The following papers cited in this review are **preprints** (not yet peer-reviewed in a journal or major conference proceedings): Kress-Gazit et al. (2024), Jiang et al. (2026), Selvaraj et al. (2026, SafeVLA-Bench), Zha et al. (2026, LAP), Petkov et al. (2026, LADDER), and Chen et al. (2026, RoboDojo). The following are **peer-reviewed**: Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L), Kimble et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L), Calli et al. (2015, IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine), Vagas et al. (2026, IEEE RA-L), Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics), Heo et al. (2025, IJRR), Luo et al. (2024, IJRR), Denoun et al. (2023, IEEE Transactions on Robotics), Morgan et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L), Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection), Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology), Cadène et al. (2026, ICLR), and Budde et al. (2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science)."}

## 1. The Problem: How the Field Currently Reports Success

The dominant metric in physical robot-manipulation evaluation is "success rate"—the percentage of autonomous runs that succeed. Kress-Gazit et al. A recent audit of the five most-cited manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0) found that the majority of reported performance gaps between policies are statistically inconclusive when examined with paired Wald tests: across LIBERO, only 20.8% of 789 comparisons were provably significant at the 5% level (jiang2026whatarewe pages 5-7).

Each manipulation trial is naturally modeled as a Bernoulli random variable X ∈ {0,1} with unknown success probability p (hietanen2021benchmarkingposeestimation pages 5-8). The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol defines reliability as "the probability of successfully completing a task or sub-task," computed from "a confidence level (CL), the number of successes (m), and the number of independent trials (n)" using the binomial cumulative distribution function (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9). This requires independent, identically distributed trials—a condition that Vincent et al. ### 2.2 Clopper–Pearson (Exact) Intervals

The Clopper–Pearson method inverts exact binomial tail probabilities to produce a confidence interval whose coverage is guaranteed to be at least 1−α for all values of p (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 3-4, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 1-3). Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics) characterizes Clopper–Pearson as "very conservative" because its actual coverage typically exceeds the nominal level, especially at small sample sizes; mean coverage at n=15 with nominal 95% was measured at 0.974 (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 8-11). Vincent et al. (2024) note that the Clopper–Pearson lower bound is obtained from their uniformly most accurate (UMA) framework by "setting U = 0 in the test statistic," confirming it as a special case of the optimal bound and showing that their randomized UMA bound is always tighter (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 3-4, vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5).

Wilson score intervals provide better-behaved coverage than the normal-approximation (Wald) interval, particularly when p is near 0 or 1 or when sample sizes are small (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3). The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark (Vagas et al. 2026, IEEE RA-L) explicitly states that "we report Wilson score confidence intervals, which offer [well-behaved coverage] when sample sizes are small or observed proportions are close to 0 or 1" (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3). Wilson intervals are increasingly adopted in 2025–2026 manipulation papers: Zhang et al. (2025, preprint) report "Wilson-score 95% confidence intervals for SR [success rate]" on their Mobile ALOHA VLA benchmarking (zhang2511experiencesfrombenchmarking pages 4-5); SafeVLA-Bench uses "Wilson score 95% intervals for binomial proportions"; and LADDER reports "95% Wilson confidence intervals over episodes."

Orawo (2021) recommends Wilson and likelihood intervals over both Wald and Clopper–Pearson for practical use, because they achieve near-nominal coverage without the excessive conservatism of the exact method (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 8-11).

### 2.4 Bayesian Approach

Kress-Gazit et al. (2024) illustrate a Bayesian alternative: model success as a Bernoulli distribution with unknown probability, place a uniform prior, and inspect the posterior distribution. They demonstrate that two policies achieving 13/20 (65%) and 14/20 (70%) have substantially overlapping posteriors, yielding only a 0.11 probability that the inferior policy is truly better—emphasizing that identical percentages from small samples cannot support superiority claims (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9, kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 9-13).

## 3. Minimum Number of Trials for Reliability Claims

The central sample-size question for robot reliability is: if all n trials succeed, how large must n be to claim that p ≥ p₀ with confidence 1−α? The exact one-sided binomial answer is n ≥ ⌈ln(α)/ln(p₀)⌉ (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6). For the canonical claim of "at least 95% success with 95% confidence," this yields n = ⌈ln(0.05)/ln(0.95)⌉ = ⌈58.40⌉ = 59 trials with zero failures. The well-known "rule of three" approximates this as 3/(1−p₀) = 60 (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6). If a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval is required instead, the lower tail uses α/2 = 0.025, yielding n = ⌈ln(0.025)/ln(0.95)⌉ = 72 (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6).

The following table provides the exact trial counts for several practically relevant reliability targets.

| Desired lower bound on success probability | Confidence level | Bound type | Required trials—all must succeed | Derivation / formula |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **59** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.95)\right\rceil=\lceil58.40\rceil=59\) (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6) |

**Critical implication for low-cost arms:** Most published manipulation papers use far fewer trials than the 59 required for a one-sided 95%/95% claim. ALOHA uses 25 real-robot trials per task (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8, zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 8-10); Mobile ALOHA uses 20 (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8); FurnitureBench uses 10 (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 6-7, heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 8-10); YCB protocols use 10 (calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulation pages 34-35, calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 34-35); and ArmnetBench uses 30 (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7). With 25 all-success trials, the one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson lower bound on p is only 0.05^(1/25) ≈ 0.887, not 0.95. To genuinely certify 95% success at 95% confidence, 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are necessary.

## 4. Mean Cycles Between Interventions and MTBF

### 4.1 In Lab Automation

Laboratory automation systems report reliability using mean time between failures (MTBF) measured in calendar days or operating hours. Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection, peer-reviewed) report that BD Kiestra TLA and WCA automated bacteriology systems achieve approximately 100 days MTBF, while the Copan WASPLab achieves approximately 95 days, with the caveat that "MTBF is difficult to specify because it depends substantially on system configuration, overall system complexity, the number and variety of samples processed each day, and user-induced factors" (croxatto2016laboratoryautomationin pages 11-13). In industrial manufacturing with Digital Twin/IIoT-enabled predictive maintenance, Mostofa (2024) reports baseline MTBF of 1,486.3 hours (SD 412.7; 95% CI [1,431.5, 1,541.1]) across 220 assets including robotic systems, improving to 2,176.8 hours post-intervention (mostofa2024digitaltwinand pages 26-27, mostofa2024digitaltwinand pages 27-29).

### 4.2 In Field Robotics

Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology, peer-reviewed) note that "the Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) for robots in field environments is often within a few hours" (honig2018understandingandresolving pages 3-5), highlighting the substantial gap between industrial automation and research robot reliability.

### 4.3 Explicit Gap: No Standard for Mean Cycles Between Interventions in Manipulation

**No published standard exists for reporting "mean cycles between interventions" (MCBI) as a reliability metric for robot manipulation tasks.** The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol uses binomial success probability and completion time (mean, SD, and 95% CI), but does not define a cycles-between-interventions metric (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9). Lab automation papers report MTBF in time units rather than task cycles (croxatto2016laboratoryautomationin pages 11-13). For teams running repeated pick-and-place or assembly cycles on low-cost arms, defining and reporting MCBI—the mean number of autonomous task cycles completed before a human must intervene to reset, fix a jam, or correct an error—would fill a genuine gap in the literature. This metric can be modeled as a geometric or negative-binomial random variable and reported with appropriate confidence intervals.

## 5. Best Practices for Reporting: A Synthesis

Based on the surveyed literature, the following reporting practices are recommended for teams benchmarking low-cost arms:

**What to report for each task:**
1. **Raw counts:** Report k successes out of n trials, not just percentages (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9, kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 1-3).
2. **Confidence interval:** Report a Wilson score 95% CI for each success proportion (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3, zhang2511experiencesfrombenchmarking pages 4-5), or a Clopper–Pearson interval if conservative coverage is preferred (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 3-4). If using Bayesian methods, show posterior distributions (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9).
3. **Success criterion:** Define success semantically and unambiguously. The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark defines success as "lifting the object at least 5 cm within 3 seconds and holding it for 3 seconds without slipping, with a 10-second timeout" (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3). FurnitureBench uses phase-completion scores alongside binary success (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 8-10). ArmnetBench uses three-way grading: successful, suboptimal, or failure (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9).
4. **Initial conditions:** Specify the randomization range, whether initial conditions are matched across policies, and whether evaluations are interleaved (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 3-5).
5. **Failure modes:** Describe observed failure modes qualitatively (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 1-3).
6. **Completion time:** Report mean, standard deviation, and 95% CI for task-completion time (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9).
7. **Trial independence:** Verify and state that trials are independent—no cherry-picking, no stopping-when-good, no environmental drift (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 3-4).

**How many trials to run:**
- For a **screening evaluation** during development: 20–30 trials per task are standard practice (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9) and will give Wilson 95% CI half-widths of roughly ±15–20 percentage points at 80% success.
- For a **formal reliability claim** of p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence: 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are required (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6).
- For **comparing two policies:** Use at least 20 trials per policy under matched initial conditions and apply a paired test or Bayesian comparison (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9, kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 9-13). Jiang et al. (2026, preprint) show that even with hundreds of comparisons, reported performance gaps are often statistically inconclusive (jiang2026whatarewe pages 5-7).

## 6. Placing Low-Cost Arms in the Published Literature

### 6.1 Available Benchmarks for SO-101 and ALOHA-Class Arms

**ArmnetBench v0.1** (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint) is the most directly relevant benchmark for SO-101 arms. It evaluates 7 policies (ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct 2) across 12 tasks on a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, using 30 rollouts per task-policy pair with 50 demonstrations and three-way operator scoring (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3).

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al. 2026, ICLR, peer-reviewed) provides the open-source software stack supporting SO-100, SO-101, Koch-v1.1, and ALOHA hardware. It integrates LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks and standardized dataset formats, but the paper itself does not report real-world success-rate benchmarks with confidence intervals for specific arms (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 10-11).

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) provides a multi-embodiment dataset spanning Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, AgileX dual-arm robot, and a humanoid, with 107k demonstrations across 479 tasks, enabling cross-embodiment comparison.

### 6.2 Explicit Gaps

- **No published peer-reviewed paper benchmarks the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm** on any standard manipulation protocol with reported confidence intervals. Any reliability claim for PiPER would need to be generated de novo.
- **No published paper provides a head-to-head reliability comparison** (with binomial confidence intervals or MTBF) between low-cost arms (SO-101, PiPER, ALOHA) and industrial arms (UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) on matched tasks. RoboMIND includes multiple embodiments but reports imitation-learning success rates rather than hardware-reliability metrics.
- **ABB YuMi** and **Kinova** arms appear in the manipulation literature but not in published benchmarks with the statistical rigor described here.

### 6.3 Repeatable Protocol Recommendation

For teams with PiPER and SO-101 arms seeking to generate publishable, comparable data:

1. **Select a standard object set** (YCB objects are freely available with 3D models) (calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 34-35).
2. **Use the NIST Assembly Task Board protocol** for assembly tasks: record start/finish times, autonomous operation only (no manual intervention permitted), and report binomial reliability bounds (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9).
3. **For imitation-learning policies**, follow the ArmnetBench protocol: 50 demonstrations, 30+ rollouts per task-policy pair, three-way scoring, randomized initial placement (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7).
4. **Report Wilson score 95% CIs** for all success proportions, state the one-sided or two-sided convention, and report raw k/n alongside percentages.
5. **For reliability certification**, run at least 59 consecutive successful trials per task to claim p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6).
6. **For comparing with Franka or UR5e results**, use matched tasks from FMB (25 trials, Franka), FurnitureBench (10 trials, Franka Panda), or RoboMIND protocols and recompute confidence intervals on the published raw counts.

## 7. Publication Status of Cited Sources

The following papers cited in this review are **preprints** (not yet peer-reviewed in a journal or major conference proceedings): Kress-Gazit et al. (2024), Jiang et al. (2026), Selvaraj et al. (2026, ArmnetBench), Wu et al. (2024, RoboMIND), Zhao et al. (2023, ALOHA), Fu et al. (2024, Mobile ALOHA), Zhang et al. (2025, Experiences Benchmarking VLA), Fan et al. (2026, SafeVLA-Bench), Zha et al. (2026, LAP), Petkov et al. (2026, LADDER), and Chen et al. (2026, RoboDojo). The following are **peer-reviewed**: Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L), Kimble et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L), Calli et al. (2015, IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine), Vagas et al. (2026, IEEE RA-L), Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics), Heo et al. (2025, IJRR), Luo et al. (2024, IJRR), Denoun et al. (2023, IEEE Transactions on Robotics), Morgan et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L), Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection), Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology), Cadène et al. (2026, ICLR), and Budde et al. (2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science).

## 2. Binomial Confidence Intervals for Binary Task Success

### 2.1 Framing the Problem

Each manipulation trial is naturally modeled as a Bernoulli random variable X ∈ {0,1} with unknown success probability p (pqac-00000007). The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol defines reliability as "the probability of successfully completing a task or sub-task," computed from "a confidence level (CL), the number of successes (m), and the number of independent trials (n)" using the binomial cumulative distribution function (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000037). This requires independent, identically distributed trials—a condition that Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L) emphasize must be ensured by a pre-specified testing plan, warning that practices such as "running policy rollouts until enough favorable outcomes are observed" violate the i.i.d. assumption (pqac-00000040).

### 2.2 Clopper–Pearson (Exact) Intervals

The Clopper–Pearson method inverts exact binomial tail probabilities to produce a confidence interval whose coverage is guaranteed to be at least 1−α for all values of p (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055). The two-sided 100(1−α)% interval allocates α/2 to each tail. Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics) characterizes Clopper–Pearson as "very conservative" because its actual coverage typically exceeds the nominal level, especially at small sample sizes; mean coverage at n=15 with nominal 95% was measured at 0.974 (pqac-00000056). Vincent et al. (2024) note that the Clopper–Pearson lower bound is obtained from their uniformly most accurate (UMA) framework by "setting U = 0 in the test statistic," confirming it as a special case of the optimal bound and showing that their randomized UMA bound is always tighter (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000051).

### 2.3 Wilson Score Intervals

Wilson score intervals provide better-behaved coverage than the normal-approximation (Wald) interval, particularly when p is near 0 or 1 or when sample sizes are small (pqac-00000016). The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark (Vagas et al. 2026, IEEE RA-L) explicitly states that "we report Wilson score confidence intervals, which offer [well-behaved coverage] when sample sizes are small or observed proportions are close to 0 or 1" (pqac-00000016). Wilson intervals are increasingly adopted in 2025–2026 manipulation papers: Zhang et al. (2025, preprint) report "Wilson-score 95% confidence intervals for SR [success rate]" on their Mobile ALOHA VLA benchmarking (pqac-00000023); SafeVLA-Bench uses "Wilson score 95% intervals for binomial proportions"; and LADDER reports "95% Wilson confidence intervals over episodes."

Orawo (2021) recommends Wilson and likelihood intervals over both Wald and Clopper–Pearson for practical use, because they achieve near-nominal coverage without the excessive conservatism of the exact method (pqac-00000056).

### 2.4 Bayesian Approach

Kress-Gazit et al. (2024) illustrate a Bayesian alternative: model success as a Bernoulli distribution with unknown probability, place a uniform prior, and inspect the posterior distribution. They demonstrate that two policies achieving 13/20 (65%) and 14/20 (70%) have substantially overlapping posteriors, yielding only a 0.11 probability that the inferior policy is truly better—emphasizing that identical percentages from small samples cannot support superiority claims (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010).

## 3. Minimum Number of Trials for Reliability Claims

The central sample-size question for robot reliability is: if all n trials succeed, how large must n be to claim that p ≥ p₀ with confidence 1−α? The exact one-sided binomial answer is n ≥ ⌈ln(α)/ln(p₀)⌉ (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053). For the canonical claim of "at least 95% success with 95% confidence," this yields n = ⌈ln(0.05)/ln(0.95)⌉ = ⌈58.40⌉ = 59 trials with zero failures. The well-known "rule of three" approximates this as 3/(1−p₀) = 60 (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). If a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval is required instead, the lower tail uses α/2 = 0.025, yielding n = ⌈ln(0.025)/ln(0.95)⌉ = 72 (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000053).

**What to report for each task:**
1. **Raw counts:** Report k successes out of n trials, not just percentages (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012).
2. **Confidence interval:** Report a Wilson score 95% CI for each success proportion (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023), or a Clopper–Pearson interval if conservative coverage is preferred (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). If using Bayesian methods, show posterior distributions (pqac-00000003).
3. **Success criterion:** Define success semantically and unambiguously. The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark defines success as "lifting the object at least 5 cm within 3 seconds and holding it for 3 seconds without slipping, with a 10-second timeout" (pqac-00000016). FurnitureBench uses phase-completion scores alongside binary success (pqac-00000062). ArmnetBench uses three-way grading: successful, suboptimal, or failure (pqac-00000058).
4. **Initial conditions:** Specify the randomization range, whether initial conditions are matched across policies, and whether evaluations are interleaved (pqac-00000013).
5. **Failure modes:** Describe observed failure modes qualitatively (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012).
6. **Completion time:** Report mean, standard deviation, and 95% CI for task-completion time (pqac-00000037).
7. **Trial independence:** Verify and state that trials are independent—no cherry-picking, no stopping-when-good, no environmental drift (pqac-00000040).

**How many trials to run:**
- For a **screening evaluation** during development: 20–30 trials per task are standard practice (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000058) and will give Wilson 95% CI half-widths of roughly ±15–20 percentage points at 80% success.
- For a **formal reliability claim** of p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence: 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are required (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052).
- For **comparing two policies:** Use at least 20 trials per policy under matched initial conditions and apply a paired test or Bayesian comparison (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000010). Jiang et al. (2026, preprint) show that even with hundreds of comparisons, reported performance gaps are often statistically inconclusive (pqac-00000042).

## 6. Placing Low-Cost Arms in the Published Literature

### 6.1 Available Benchmarks for SO-101 and ALOHA-Class Arms

**ArmnetBench v0.1** (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint) is the most directly relevant benchmark for SO-101 arms. It evaluates 7 policies (ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct 2) across 12 tasks on a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, using 30 rollouts per task-policy pair with 50 demonstrations and three-way operator scoring (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060).

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al. 2026, ICLR, peer-reviewed) provides the open-source software stack supporting SO-100, SO-101, Koch-v1.1, and ALOHA hardware. It integrates LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks and standardized dataset formats, but the paper itself does not report real-world success-rate benchmarks with confidence intervals for specific arms (pqac-00000046).

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) provides a multi-embodiment dataset spanning Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, AgileX dual-arm robot, and a humanoid, with 107k demonstrations across 479 tasks, enabling cross-embodiment comparison.

### 6.2 Explicit Gaps

- **No published peer-reviewed paper benchmarks the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm** on any standard manipulation protocol with reported confidence intervals. Any reliability claim for PiPER would need to be generated de novo.
- **No published paper provides a head-to-head reliability comparison** (with binomial confidence intervals or MTBF) between low-cost arms (SO-101, PiPER, ALOHA) and industrial arms (UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) on matched tasks. RoboMIND includes multiple embodiments but reports imitation-learning success rates rather than hardware-reliability metrics.
- **ABB YuMi** and **Kinova** arms appear in the manipulation literature but not in published benchmarks with the statistical rigor described here.

### 6.3 Repeatable Protocol Recommendation

For teams with PiPER and SO-101 arms seeking to generate publishable, comparable data:

1. **Select a standard object set** (YCB objects are freely available with 3D models) (pqac-00000015).
2. **Use the NIST Assembly Task Board protocol** for assembly tasks: record start/finish times, autonomous operation only (no manual intervention permitted), and report binomial reliability bounds (pqac-00000037).
3. **For imitation-learning policies**, follow the ArmnetBench protocol: 50 demonstrations, 30+ rollouts per task-policy pair, three-way scoring, randomized initial placement (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059).
4. **Report Wilson score 95% CIs** for all success proportions, state the one-sided or two-sided convention, and report raw k/n alongside percentages.
5. **For reliability certification**, run at least 59 consecutive successful trials per task to claim p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052).
6. **For comparing with Franka or UR5e results**, use matched tasks from FMB (25 trials, Franka), FurnitureBench (10 trials, Franka Panda), or RoboMIND protocols and recompute confidence intervals on the published raw counts.

contexts.context: The excerpt recommends reporting robot-manipulation success as a statistically justified lower confidence bound on the unknown probability of task success, rather than reporting only the observed success percentage. Confidence and tightness should be stated explicitly: confidence describes how often the bound covers the true success probability, while tightness describes how close the bound tends to be to that probability. For binary success/failure outcomes, the paper revisits the Clopper–Pearson approach and presents a tighter binomial bound that can achieve a user-specified confidence level while minimizing rollouts. The method is distribution-free and does not depend on robot state dimensionality, observation dimensionality, policy structure, hardware, or environment physics, but it assumes independent and identically distributed performance measurements. The excerpt also emphasizes the trade-off among confidence, tightness, and sample size. It does not provide the numerical trial count for claiming 95% success with 95% confidence, nor does it discuss Wilson intervals specifically. That number therefore requires selecting a convention—such as a one-sided versus two-sided interval—and calculating the relevant binomial lower bound, typically assuming all observed trials succeed.

contexts.context: The excerpt recommends evaluating manipulation policies with an explicitly defined performance metric, such as binary task success/failure or continuous reward, and warns that reporting only an empirical success rate from a small number of rollouts can make statistical significance difficult to interpret. It motivates reporting confidence-based lower bounds on performance, especially when safety or reliability matters. The proposed framework uses policy rollouts in the environment of interest, converts each rollout into a binary or continuous measurement, and computes an upper confidence bound on the cumulative distribution function; for binary success, this corresponds to a confidence bound on the success probability. The paper compares its bounds with established approaches, including Clopper–Pearson and DKW bounds, and reports improved tightness for small sample sizes. It also emphasizes user-specified confidence and tightness, and direct testing in out-of-distribution environments. However, these pages do not state the exact minimum number of trials required to claim a 95% success rate with 95% confidence, nor do they provide a specific Wilson-versus-Clopper–Pearson reporting rule. That numerical requirement would need to be derived from the chosen one-sided or two-sided confidence-interval definition and the observed number of successes.
contexts.question: How should success rates and confidence intervals (Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, binomial) be reported for robot manipulation tasks? What is the minimum number of trials needed to claim 95% success rate with 95% confidence?

contexts.context: The excerpt models robot-task outcomes as Bernoulli trials: each manipulation attempt is either successful (X = 1) or unsuccessful (X = 0), with success probability p. For homogeneous trials, the maximum-likelihood estimate of the success rate is the observed sample average, i.e., the number of successes divided by the number of trials. The paper cautions that pose-dependent manipulation trials are generally non-homogeneous because success probability varies with the object pose and depends on factors such as object shape, gripper properties, and task requirements. Consequently, a simple pooled binomial estimate is only directly justified when trials share a common success probability, or when an appropriate model accounts for variation. This excerpt does not specify Wilson, Clopper–Pearson, or other confidence-interval procedures, nor does it provide a minimum trial count for claiming a 95% success rate with 95% confidence. Determining that count requires an explicit statistical convention—particularly whether the claim means an exact observed rate of 95%, a lower confidence bound of at least 95%, or a one-sided binomial guarantee—and assumptions about independent, identically distributed trials.
contexts.question: How should success rates and confidence intervals (Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, binomial) be reported for robot manipulation tasks? What is the minimum number of trials needed to claim 95% success rate with 95% confidence?

contexts.context: The excerpt defines reliability for robot manipulation and assembly tasks as the probability of successfully completing a task or sub-task. Success-rate reporting should therefore identify the number of successful outcomes (m), the total number of independent trials (n), and the confidence level (CL), using the binomial cumulative distribution function to establish a confidence-based bound on the success probability. The protocol also requires repeated trials and recommends reporting the mean, standard deviation, and 95% confidence interval for completion times; the excerpt does not specify whether Wilson, Clopper–Pearson, or another interval should be used for proportions. For a claim of at least 95% success with 95% confidence when every trial succeeds, the standard one-sided exact binomial calculation requires 59 independent trials: 0.95^n ≤ 0.05. If a two-sided 95% interval is required, the corresponding exact lower-bound calculation is more conservative and requires 73 all-success trials. These trial counts assume zero observed failures and should be stated explicitly, along with the interval method and whether the confidence bound is one- or two-sided. The protocol emphasizes keeping the task-board variant constant when comparing systems.
contexts.question: How should success rates and confidence intervals (Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, binomial) be reported for robot manipulation tasks? What is the minimum number of trials needed to claim 95% success rate with 95% confidence?

contexts.context: The excerpt recommends that robot-manipulation papers report success rates together with the raw number of successful and total trials, rather than percentages alone. It gives a concrete example: policy A succeeds in 15 of 18 trials (83.3%), while policy B succeeds in 11 of 17 trials (64.7%). The authors emphasize that identical percentages can support very different conclusions depending on the number of evaluations: fewer trials make conclusions weaker, while more trials make them stronger. They also recommend statistical analysis rather than relying only on point estimates. This can involve frequentist interval estimates or bounds, or Bayesian estimation of the success-probability distribution. In the Bayesian example, the overlap between policy distributions indicates uncertainty, and the analysis estimates only an 0.11 probability that policy B performs better than policy A. The provided excerpt does not identify typical trial counts for ALOHA, LeRobot, Franka, or UR5e evaluations, nor does it compare reporting conventions across those platforms. It therefore supports general reporting guidance and one example of specific trial counts, but not platform-specific norms or a survey of whether those evaluations report confidence intervals.
